day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Lisbon Airport at 13:00 — no morning activities scheduled. Clear customs, collect luggage, and take the Metro (Linha Vermelha/Red Line) from Aeroporto station to the city center. Budget tip: a single Metro ticket costs around €1.50, or grab a rechargeable Viva Viagem card for €0.50 plus credit.
day_by_day.afternoon: Check in to Lisbon City Stay and freshen up. Once settled, take a leisurely walk through the Baixa (Downtown) district to get your bearings. Stroll along Rua Augusta pedestrian street, admire the Arco da Rua Augusta (free to view from outside), and head down to Praça do Comércio overlooking the Tagus River — all free to explore and a perfect low-key introduction to Lisbon's historic core.
day_by_day.evening: Head to the Alfama neighborhood for your first taste of authentic Lisbon. Wander the narrow medieval alleyways, climb up to the Miradouro de Santa Luzia viewpoint (free) for a golden-hour view over the rooftops and river. Listen for live Fado music drifting from local tascas as the evening sets in.

meals.breakfast: Grab a quick snack at the airport or skip — you arrive at 13:00.
meals.lunch: Pick up a fresh bifana (pork sandwich) or a pastel de bacalhau (salt cod cake) from a local bakery or street stall near Baixa for €1.50–€3. Try Padaria São Roque or any neighborhood padaria.
meals.dinner: Dine at a traditional tasca in Alfama such as Tasca do Chico or a similar neighborhood spot. Look for a prato do dia (dish of the day) which typically includes soup, main, bread, and a drink for €8–€12.

day_by_day.notes: Day 1 is intentionally relaxed given the midday arrival. Focus on orientation and soaking in the atmosphere rather than rushing to monuments. Validate your Metro card and keep it for the whole trip — it saves money versus single tickets.

day_by_day.morning: Start the day with a visit to the São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge). Tickets are around €15 but book online in advance for a small discount. The castle sits atop Alfama hill with panoramic views over all of Lisbon and the Tagus. Explore the ramparts, towers, and the small archaeological museum inside. Allow 2–2.5 hours.
day_by_day.afternoon: Descend from the castle and spend the afternoon exploring the Alfama district on foot — the oldest neighborhood in Lisbon, dating back to Moorish times. Visit the Sé de Lisboa (Lisbon Cathedral), which is free to enter the main nave. Browse the Feira da Ladra flea market at Campo de Santa Clara if it falls on a Tuesday or Saturday (it does today!) — great for cheap vintage finds and people-watching.
day_by_day.evening: Experience the Time Out Market Lisbon Food Tour experience. Head to Mercado da Ribeira (Time Out Market) in Cais do Sodré. Spend the evening grazing through stalls from Lisbon's top chefs — try petiscos (Portuguese tapas), fresh seafood, local cheeses, and pastries. Budget smartly by sharing dishes and sticking to 2–3 stalls.

meals.breakfast: Start at a neighborhood café near the hotel — a galão (milky espresso) and a tosta mista (toasted ham and cheese sandwich) costs around €2–€3. Try any local café rather than tourist-facing spots.
meals.lunch: Grab a light lunch near the Feira da Ladra — look for a simple café offering soup and a sandwich for under €6, or pick up snacks from market vendors.
meals.dinner: Dinner IS the Time Out Market experience. Budget €12–€18 for a satisfying grazing dinner across multiple stalls. Pair with a glass of local vinho verde (green wine) for €3–€4.

day_by_day.notes: Wear comfortable walking shoes — Alfama involves steep cobblestone streets and significant elevation changes. The Feira da Ladra runs Tuesdays and Saturdays, so today is a lucky timing. Arrive at Time Out Market before 19:00 on weekends to beat the crowds.

day_by_day.morning: Take Tram 15E or a direct bus from Praça da Figueira to Belém (about 30 minutes, ~€1.50 with your Viva Viagem card). Begin with the Belém Historical Monuments experience: visit the UNESCO-listed Jerónimos Monastery, a breathtaking example of Manueline Gothic architecture built in the 16th century. Entry is €10 (reduced/free on Sunday mornings before 14:00 for EU citizens — check current policy). Allow 1.5–2 hours inside.
day_by_day.afternoon: Walk along the riverside promenade to the iconic Torre de Belém (Tower of Belém), another Manueline masterpiece and UNESCO World Heritage Site. Entry is around €6. Nearby, also view the Monument to the Discoveries (Padrão dos Descobrimentos) from the outside for free. The entire Belém riverside area is beautiful for a walk along the Tagus.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon via tram or bus. Spend the evening in the Chiado and Bairro Alto neighborhoods — Chiado is elegant and literary (visit the statue of Fernando Pessoa outside Café A Brasileira), while Bairro Alto comes alive at night with affordable bars and petiscos restaurants.

meals.breakfast: This is non-negotiable: stop at the original Pastéis de Belém bakery (open since 1837) for the world-famous pastel de nata custard tarts, freshly baked and dusted with cinnamon. Two tarts cost around €2.40 — pair with a bica (espresso) for a perfect Lisbon breakfast.
meals.lunch: Pack a picnic or grab takeaway near Belém — a prego no pão (steak sandwich) or a simple snack from a local café for €4–€7. Eat by the riverside gardens.
meals.dinner: Explore Bairro Alto's affordable restaurant row. Many spots offer a two-course menu with wine for €10–€14. Look for places with handwritten menus and locals dining inside — a good sign of authenticity and value.

day_by_day.notes: Belém is about 6–7 km from central Lisbon. The Tram 15E is the most scenic route but can be crowded on weekends — Bus 728 or 729 is faster and less touristy. Confirm monastery free-entry hours for Sunday before you go, as policies can change seasonally.

day_by_day.morning: Dedicate the morning to the National Tile Museum (Museu Nacional do Azulejo), one of Lisbon's most unique and underrated museums. Located in a former 16th-century convent in the Xabregas neighborhood, it traces five centuries of Portuguese azulejo (decorative tile) art. Entry is around €5 (free on the first Sunday of the month — not today, but still great value). Allow 2–2.5 hours. Take Bus 718 or 742 from central Lisbon.
day_by_day.afternoon: Head back toward central Lisbon and explore the Mouraria neighborhood — the historic Moorish quarter adjacent to Alfama, one of Lisbon's oldest and most multicultural areas. Visit the free Intendente Square (Largo do Intendente), recently renovated and full of local character. Browse the area's small shops, street art, and hidden miradouros (viewpoints). Stop at Miradouro da Graça for sweeping city views.
day_by_day.evening: Take the historic Elevador da Bica or Elevador da Glória funicular (€3.80 round trip, or free with a Lisboa Card if you have one) up to the Bairro Alto for a relaxed evening. Explore the area's independent bookshops, vintage stores, and settle into a cervejaria (beer hall) or wine bar for a low-key evening of local wine and petiscos.

meals.breakfast: Have breakfast near the hotel before heading out — a café with a croissant or pão de leite (sweet bread roll) and coffee for €2–€3.
meals.lunch: Try a local restaurant in Mouraria for a hearty and cheap prato do dia. The area around Intendente Square has several affordable spots serving traditional Portuguese food for €7–€10 including bread, soup, main, and a drink.
meals.dinner: Visit a tasca in Bairro Alto for petiscos-style dining — order several small plates to share, such as chouriço assado (grilled sausage), queijo da serra (mountain cheese), and pão com manteiga (bread and butter). Budget €10–€15 per person with a glass of wine.

day_by_day.notes: The Tile Museum is easily one of the most rewarding experiences in Lisbon for history and art lovers and is far less crowded than the main tourist sites. The convent's Baroque chapel inside is stunning and often overlooked. Check the museum's website for any temporary exhibitions running during your visit.

day_by_day.morning: Spend your final morning in the Príncipe Real neighborhood — one of Lisbon's most charming and elegant districts, with a beautiful garden square (Jardim do Príncipe Real), antique shops, and independent boutiques. Browse the Saturday market (today is Tuesday, but the area is still lovely for a morning stroll). Visit the Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara (free) for a panoramic final view of the city skyline and the castle.
day_by_day.afternoon: Head to the Museu do Dinheiro (Museum of Money) in Baixa — housed in a stunning former church and bank building, it's free to enter and offers a fascinating look at Portuguese economic history and the evolution of money. Afterward, walk along the waterfront promenade at Ribeira das Naus, a reconstructed 16th-century shipyard by the Tagus — free, scenic, and perfect for a last afternoon in the sun.
day_by_day.evening: Return to the hotel to pack and prepare for departure. Spend your last evening in Lisbon with a farewell dinner in Baixa or Cais do Sodré — somewhere that encapsulates everything you've loved about the city. Raise a glass of ginjinha (sour cherry liqueur, €1.50 a shot at street kiosks) as a final toast to Lisbon.

meals.breakfast: Treat yourself to a slightly more indulgent final breakfast — head to Café A Brasileira in Chiado (open since 1905) for a galão and a pastel de nata in a historic literary setting. Budget €4–€5.
meals.lunch: Grab a quick and cheap lunch at a cervejaria or snack bar in Príncipe Real or Bairro Alto — a prawn or crab sandwich (sanduíche de camarão) is a classic Lisbon lunch for €5–€8.
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner at a traditional cervejaria or marisqueira (seafood restaurant) near the waterfront. Try grilled sardines (sardinhas grelhadas) or bacalhau à brás (shredded salt cod with eggs and potatoes) — quintessential Lisbon dishes. Budget €12–€18 for a full meal with wine.

day_by_day.notes: If your departure flight is early on May 20th, pack the night before and confirm your airport transfer. The Metro Red Line from central Lisbon to the airport runs frequently and costs around €1.50 — far cheaper than a taxi (€15–€20). Keep your Viva Viagem card loaded for the airport journey. Overall trip tip: a Lisboa Card (24h/48h/72h) can save money on transport and museum entries if you plan to visit many paid sites in a single day.

day_by_day.morning: Arrival — Flight TP lands at 13:00, so no morning activities scheduled. Travel from Humberto Delgado Airport to Lisbon City Stay hotel via Aerobus (Line 1) or Metro (Red Line to Green Line). Check in, freshen up, and get oriented with a short stroll around your neighborhood.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore the immediate surroundings on foot — walk along Avenida da Liberdade or head down to Baixa-Chiado to get a feel for the city. Visit Praça do Comércio (Commerce Square) by the Tagus River for a relaxed introduction to Lisbon's grand architecture and waterfront atmosphere. No booking needed, completely free.
day_by_day.evening: Alfama District Walking Tour & Fado Show — Join an early-evening guided walk through Lisbon's oldest and most atmospheric neighborhood, winding through narrow cobblestone streets, past colorful tiled facades and ancient miradouros (viewpoints). The tour concludes with a live Fado performance, the soulful music that defines Lisbon's spirit. Book in advance.

meals.breakfast: Grab a coffee and pastel de nata at a café near the airport or hotel upon arrival — try a local pastelaria rather than a chain.
meals.lunch: Light meal near the hotel or airport transit — A Cevicheria or a simple tasca in Baixa for a €12–16 lunch menu (prato do dia).
meals.dinner: Dinner is typically included or follows the Fado show experience in Alfama. If not, try Taberna da Rua das Flores (Chiado) for traditional petiscos and wine, budget around €25–35 per person.

day_by_day.notes: Arrival day — keep the pace relaxed. Validate your NFC transport card (Viva Viagem) at the airport Metro station for easy travel all week. The Fado experience is the highlight; confirm your booking before departure.

day_by_day.morning: National Tile Museum (Museu Nacional do Azulejo) — Start the day with a visit to one of Lisbon's most unique cultural treasures. Spend 2–3 hours exploring five centuries of Portuguese azulejo tile art housed in a stunning 16th-century convent. The panoramic tile panel of pre-earthquake Lisbon is unmissable. Opens at 10:00; entry ~€5.
day_by_day.afternoon: Mouraria & Intendente Neighborhood Food & History Walk — After the museum, head to Mouraria, Lisbon's historic Moorish quarter and multicultural heart. Join a local guide for a walking food and history tour through this vibrant, lesser-touristed neighborhood. Sample local bites from traditional tascas, spice shops, and community eateries while learning about the area's layered history from Moorish times to today.
day_by_day.evening: Wander up to Miradouro da Graça or Miradouro da Senhora do Monte for golden-hour sunset views over the city's rooftops and the Tagus River. Afterward, enjoy a relaxed evening dinner in the Intendente or Anjos area.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel or at a neighborhood café — coffee, toast with butter and jam, and a pastel de nata for under €5.
meals.lunch: Light snacks and tastings are included during the Mouraria Food & History Walk — supplement with a bifanas (pork sandwich) or caldo verde from a local vendor.
meals.dinner: Tasca do Chico in Mouraria or Zé da Mouraria for hearty Portuguese classics like bacalhau à brás or grilled sardines. Budget €20–30 per person with wine.

day_by_day.notes: The Tile Museum is closed on Mondays, so Sunday is the perfect day. Wear comfortable walking shoes — Mouraria has steep, uneven streets. The food walk typically lasts 3 hours; book ahead as group sizes are small.

day_by_day.morning: Belém Historical Monuments — Take Tram 15E or the train from Cais do Sodré to Belém (about 20 minutes). Begin with the Jerónimos Monastery, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and masterpiece of Manueline Gothic architecture. Explore the ornate cloisters and the church where Vasco da Gama is buried. Then walk to the iconic Tower of Belém on the riverbank. Allow 3 hours total. Entry to monastery ~€10, tower ~€6.
day_by_day.afternoon: Pastéis de Belém — No visit to Belém is complete without eating the original pastel de Belém at the historic Pastéis de Belém bakery (since 1837), just steps from the monastery. Then visit the Monument to the Discoveries (Padrão dos Descobrimentos) and stroll along the riverside promenade. Optional: visit the Berardo Museum of Modern Art (free on Sundays, €5 Mon–Sat) if energy allows.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon and explore the Chiado and Bairro Alto neighborhoods. Browse independent bookshops like Livraria Bertrand (the world's oldest operating bookshop) and enjoy the lively evening atmosphere of Bairro Alto.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel, then a mid-morning snack of the famous Pastéis de Belém (€1.50 each) with a bica (espresso) — this is a must-do ritual.
meals.lunch: Lunch in Belém at Solar dos Presuntos or Cervejaria Ramiro (for seafood lovers) — alternatively, a simpler option is Taberna de Belém for petiscos. Budget €15–22.
meals.dinner: Dinner in Bairro Alto or Chiado — try Taberna da Rua das Flores or O Corvo for modern Portuguese cuisine. Budget €25–35 per person.

day_by_day.notes: Belém is about 6 km west of central Lisbon — Tram 15E is scenic but can be crowded; the Cascais commuter train from Cais do Sodré is faster. Arrive at Jerónimos Monastery early (opens 10:00) to beat tour groups. Belém gets busy by midday on weekdays.

day_by_day.morning: Time Out Market Lisbon Food Tour — Spend a leisurely late morning at Lisbon's iconic food hall in the Ribeira Market building near Cais do Sodré. Sample dishes from the best local chefs and producers: from grilled octopus and bifanas to ginjinha and artisan cheeses. This is one of the world's top food markets and a fantastic way to experience the breadth of Portuguese cuisine in one place. Budget €20–30 for grazing.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore the LX Factory — a short walk or Uber from the market, this repurposed 19th-century industrial complex in Alcântara houses independent shops, art studios, restaurants, and a famous Sunday market (though Tuesday offers a quieter, more local experience). Browse concept stores, street art, and grab a coffee at one of the creative cafés. Then walk along the Tagus riverside promenade back toward Cais do Sodré.
day_by_day.evening: São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge) — Visit this Moorish hilltop castle at dusk for spectacular panoramic views over Lisbon, the Tagus, and the 25 de Abril Bridge. The castle grounds are beautiful in the late afternoon light. Entry ~€15. Afterward, descend into the Alfama for a final evening stroll.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel or a neighborhood café. Try a tosta mista (ham and cheese toast) and galão (milky coffee) — a classic Portuguese start for under €4.
meals.lunch: Lunch IS the Time Out Market experience — graze on multiple small dishes from different stalls. Highlights include Henrique Sá Pessoa's grilled octopus and Manteigaria's pastéis de nata.
meals.dinner: Dinner in Alfama after the castle visit — try Tasca do Chico (book ahead, small venue) or A Baiuca for traditional Fado dinner. Budget €25–35 per person.

day_by_day.notes: Time Out Market is busiest at peak lunch hours (12:30–14:00) — arrive at 11:30 to get ahead of the crowds. LX Factory has its famous Sunday market, but weekday visits are more relaxed and authentic. The castle is best visited in the late afternoon for golden light and fewer tour groups.

day_by_day.morning: Sintra Day Trip (Optional) or Parque das Nações — If you're up for a half-day excursion, take the 40-minute train from Rossio station to the magical UNESCO-listed town of Sintra to see the colorful Pena Palace and Moorish Castle perched in the forested hills. Alternatively, stay in Lisbon and visit the futuristic Parque das Nações (Park of Nations), built for Expo 98, featuring the impressive Oceanarium (€22), riverside promenades, and striking contemporary architecture.
day_by_day.afternoon: Return to central Lisbon for a final afternoon of leisurely exploration. Revisit your favorite neighborhood — perhaps Príncipe Real for its antique market, garden, and upscale boutiques, or Intendente for a final coffee at a local café. Pick up souvenirs: azulejo tiles, Portuguese wine, conservas (tinned fish), or ginjinha liqueur.
day_by_day.evening: Farewell dinner — treat yourself to a slightly elevated final meal at a well-regarded Lisbon restaurant. Celebrate the trip with a proper Portuguese feast before preparing for departure.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel — fuel up well before the day trip or final explorations.
meals.lunch: If in Sintra: lunch at Tasca do Chico in the village center or a picnic with local cheeses and bread from a deli. If staying in Lisbon: lunch at Solar dos Presuntos in Restauradores for classic Lisbon cuisine — budget €18–25.
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner at Alma (Chiado) or Cervejaria Ramiro (seafood institution, no reservations, expect a wait) — budget €35–50 per person for a memorable final meal. Pair with a local vinho verde or Alentejo red.

day_by_day.notes: If flying out on May 20, pack the night before and confirm airport transfer. Sintra trains run frequently from Rossio (not Oriente) — buy a combined Lisbon+Sintra day ticket (~€10). The Oceanarium in Parque das Nações is excellent for families or ocean enthusiasts. Keep the final evening relaxed to avoid post-trip fatigue.

day_by_day.evening: Explore the vibrant LX Factory, a repurposed industrial complex that comes alive on Sundays with artisan markets, art installations, and rooftop bars. Enjoy sundowner cocktails with views over the 25 de Abril Bridge.

meals.lunch: Lunch is embedded in the Time Out Market Food Tour — enjoy a curated selection of Lisbon's finest bites across multiple stalls and chef counters
meals.dinner: Dinner at Tasca do Chico in Madragoa — an intimate, reservation-only tasca beloved for its honest, soulful Portuguese cooking and spontaneous live Fado; or opt for Prado restaurant for seasonal farm-to-table Portuguese cuisine with a sophisticated wine list

day_by_day.notes: The Tile Museum is quieter on Sunday mornings — arrive early for the best experience. LX Factory's Sunday market runs until early evening and is a wonderful way to pick up artisan souvenirs and local products.

day_by_day.morning: Mouraria & Intendente Neighborhood Food & History Walk — Join a local expert guide for an immersive walking tour through Mouraria, Lisbon's historic Moorish quarter and the birthplace of Fado. Discover hidden alleyways, ancient mosques-turned-churches, and the multicultural layers of the city's identity. Visit the beautifully restored Intendente square and its surrounding artisan workshops.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit the São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge) perched above the city for sweeping panoramic views of Lisbon's rooftops, the Tagus River, and beyond. Explore the medieval ramparts and archaeological museum within the castle grounds. Afterward, descend through the Graça neighborhood and visit the Miradouro da Graça viewpoint.
day_by_day.evening: Private sunset experience at Miradouro de Santa Catarina or Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara with a bottle of chilled Vinho Verde, arranged by your hotel concierge. Then head to a premium dinner in Príncipe Real.

meals.lunch: Lunch at Taberna da Rua das Flores in Chiado — a beloved, intimate restaurant serving traditional Portuguese petiscos and regional wines in a rustic-chic setting; reserve ahead
meals.dinner: Dinner at Antiqvvm — a Michelin-starred restaurant set in a romantic garden in Príncipe Real, offering creative Portuguese haute cuisine with exceptional wine pairings and city views

day_by_day.notes: Wear comfortable shoes for the Mouraria walk and the castle visit — both involve uneven terrain and inclines. The Mouraria tour is best experienced with a local guide who can unlock stories and spots not found in guidebooks.

day_by_day.morning: Leisurely final morning — sleep in and enjoy a long, indulgent breakfast at the hotel. Take a private wine and olive oil tasting experience arranged through the hotel concierge, or visit the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga (National Museum of Ancient Art) for a world-class collection of Portuguese paintings, gold artifacts, and Asian treasures from the Age of Discovery.
day_by_day.afternoon: Final afternoon at leisure — browse the upscale boutiques and concept stores of Chiado and Príncipe Real for premium Portuguese products: handcrafted leather goods, azulejo tiles, vintage port wines, and artisan ceramics. Visit the iconic A Vida Portuguesa shop for beautifully curated traditional Portuguese goods.
day_by_day.evening: Farewell dinner at a top Lisbon restaurant, celebrating the end of a remarkable trip with the finest Portuguese cuisine and wine.

meals.breakfast: Extended luxury breakfast at the hotel — take your time and savor it
meals.lunch: Lunch at Solar dos Presuntos — a Lisbon institution since 1974, celebrated for its traditional northern Portuguese recipes, exceptional presunto (cured ham), and warm family hospitality
meals.dinner: Grand farewell dinner at Belcanto (two Michelin stars, Chef José Avillez) in Chiado — one of Portugal's most celebrated restaurants offering a theatrical tasting menu that reinterprets the soul of Portuguese cuisine with extraordinary creativity and precision

day_by_day.notes: Belcanto is one of the most prestigious reservations in all of Portugal — book as far in advance as possible, ideally months ahead. Arrange a private luxury transfer to the airport for your departure. Ask your hotel concierge to assist with any last-minute luggage storage, gift wrapping, or packing services.

query: Lisbon city break, $2500 couple, food and history, 5 days, May 2027, from Boston
